titleText.es: Todos los hilos de ayuda largos deberían tener arriba un post
titleText.en: All long help threads should have a sticky globally-editable post at the top saying 'DEAR PEOPLE FROM THE FUTURE: Here's what we've figured out so far ...'
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive title attribute is preserved exactly, including its trailing space and truncation after post; the raw page's malformed quoted text prevents the remainder from appearing in the manifest. The official English title attribute is preserved exactly. Vision omitted the accent in QUIÉN, and GOOGLE, DENVERCODER9, and 2003 are inventoried as non-lexical exclusions.

regions.labelEs: NUNCA ME HE SENTIDO TAN CERCANO A OTRO SER

applications.explanationEn: He is the present helper for the speaker, and sentido is the irregular completed-action form of sentir.
Me and sentido form sentirse for the speaker, while tan cercano describes the resulting feeling.
Tan raises the degree of the description cercano.
Cercano gives the description, a introduces its complement, and otro ser names what the speaker feels close to.

regions.labelEs: Y SIN EMBARGO TAN SOLO COMO CUANDO BUSCO UN ERROR EN GOOGLE

excludedUnits.rationale: This search-engine product name is not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Sin and embargo form the fixed contrast connector.
Tan introduces the degree, solo supplies the description, and como introduces the comparison point.

regions.labelEs: UN HILO INICIADO POR ALGUIEN CON EL MISMO PROBLEMA

applications.explanationEn: Iniciado follows hilo to describe the thread as one that was started.
The masculine singular ending -ado agrees with hilo.
Sin establishes the absence, respuesta names what is missing, and postposed alguna strengthens it to ‘none at all.’

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed year is an Arabic numeral rather than a Spanish lexical word.
This alphanumeric username is not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Quién keeps its written accent because it directly asks for a person's identity.
Qué keeps its accent because it directly asks what was seen.
Lo and que together introduce the unnamed thing identified by the following action.
Has is the present helper for one familiar listener, and visto is the completed-action form of ver.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.en: I complain about the noise.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe how a person feels?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of sentirse followed by a describing word.
cards.noteEn: The describing word normally changes to agree with the person: cansado for a man, cansada for a woman, and plural forms for more than one person.

example.en: We feel calm.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Sentido is the irregular completed-action form of sentir. With a matching short word such as me and the helper haber, it describes how someone has felt.

example.es: Nunca me he sentido tan tranquilo.
example.en: I have never felt so calm.

cards.promptEs: error · un resultado · hilo · sin respuesta · DenverCoder9
cards.questionEn: Why does the old unanswered thread feel like contact with a lost person?
cards.answerEn: A highly specific search finds one old post from someone with the same problem, but the thread contains no solution or later trace of its author.
cards.noteEn: The emotional joke treats an abandoned technical-help thread like an ancient message. The official title text imagines a prominent, editable summary that future visitors could update with whatever has been learned.

cards.questionEn: How do you intensify a describing word to mean “so,” as in “so difficult”?
cards.answerEn: Put tan immediately before the word that describes the person, thing, or action.
cards.noteEn: Tan does not change form. It goes before an adjective, a word that describes a person or thing, or before an adverb, a word that describes an action. Use forms of tanto instead before a noun or when saying “so much” or “so many.”

example.en: The exam was so difficult.

cards.noteEn: Cercano can describe physical nearness or a close emotional connection. It changes to cercana, cercanos, or cercanas to agree with the person or thing described.

example.es: Me siento cercano a mi familia.
example.en: I feel close to my family.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is close to another person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of cercano followed by a.
cards.noteEn: Cercano changes to agree with what is described, while a introduces the person, place, or thing it is close to.

example.es: La estación está cercana al centro.
example.en: The station is close to downtown.

cards.answerEn: to; required after cercano before the person or thing
cards.noteEn: Cercano normally uses a before naming what someone or something is close to. English also commonly uses ‘to’ here.

example.es: El pueblo está cercano a la costa.
example.en: The town is close to the coast.

cards.noteEn: Ser usually appears as the dictionary form “to be.” With an article, el ser can instead be a noun meaning a being, existence, or the self.

example.es: El ensayo reflexiona sobre el ser.
example.en: The essay reflects on being.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sin embargo (“however”)
cards.noteEn: Sin normally means “without,” but sin embargo is one fixed connector. In that expression, translate the pair together rather than translating sin separately.

example.en: I wanted to go out; however, it was raining.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a contrast with “however” or “nevertheless”?
cards.answerEn: Use sin embargo before or after the contrasting idea.
cards.noteEn: Sin embargo functions as one fixed connector. Its meaning is not obtained by translating sin as “without” and embargo separately. A comma often separates it from the rest of the statement.

example.es: Está cansada; sin embargo, continúa trabajando.
example.en: She is tired; however, she keeps working.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sin embargo (“however”)
cards.noteEn: In sin embargo, embargo does not contribute a separate English word. The two Spanish words work together as the connector “however” or “nevertheless.”

example.es: Es difícil; sin embargo, es posible.
example.en: It is difficult; however, it is possible.

cards.answerEn: as (before a description in tan… como)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that two things are equally strong in some quality?
cards.answerEn: Put tan before the describing word and como before the comparison: tan… como means “as… as.”
cards.noteEn: A describing word can describe a thing, such as claro (“clear”), or how an action happens, such as rápido (“quickly”). Tan and como stay unchanged; only the surrounding words change as the surrounding grammar requires.

example.es: El café está tan frío como el agua.
example.en: The coffee is as cold as the water.

cards.noteEn: When solo describes a masculine person's state, it means alone or lonely rather than “only.” The feminine form is sola.

example.es: Se sintió solo en la ciudad nueva.
example.en: He felt lonely in the new city.

cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

example.en: She runs like her brother.

cards.answerEn: I search for; I look up
cards.noteEn: Busco is the present form of buscar used by the speaker. The spelling uses c before o.

example.en: I search for the answer online.

cards.noteEn: Spanish uses en before a website, app, or online service where something happens. English commonly uses “on” in the same setting.

example.es: Vi el anuncio en una página web.
example.en: I saw the advertisement on a website.

cards.noteEn: Sale is a form of salir. Depending on the setting, salir can mean to leave, to come out, or to appear. Here it describes something suddenly appearing.

example.es: De pronto sale un actor al escenario.
example.en: Suddenly, an actor appears onstage.

cards.noteEn: Resultado names an outcome. In an online search, it can mean one returned result or listing.

example.es: La búsqueda dio un solo resultado.
example.en: The search returned only one result.

cards.noteEn: Hilo literally means ‘thread.’ Online, it names a connected discussion made of an opening post and its replies.

example.es: Leí todo el hilo del foro.
example.en: I read the whole forum thread.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Iniciado is the masculine singular completed-action form of iniciar. Used after a noun, it describes something that was started.

example.es: Es un proyecto iniciado en mayo.
example.en: It is a project started in May.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish emphasize that there is no item of a certain kind at all?
cards.answerEn: Use sin, name the missing thing, and put a matching form of alguno after the noun.
cards.noteEn: After sin, postposed alguno adds strong negative force: sin motivo alguno and sin respuesta alguna. The ending agrees with the noun. English normally uses ‘any’ or ‘at all.’

example.en: There was no change at all.

cards.noteEn: Respuesta can be an answer to a question or a reply in a conversation or online discussion.

example.en: There is still no answer.

cards.answerEn: any; at all (after a noun in a negative expression)
cards.noteEn: After a negative idea such as sin, alguno can follow the noun and strengthens the absence: sin respuesta alguna means no answer at all. It agrees with the noun, so feminine respuesta takes alguna.

example.en: She left without any explanation.

cards.noteEn: Publicado is the masculine singular completed-action form of publicar. It can describe material made public online as well as in print.

example.en: The article was published yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Before a specific moment, en can correspond to English “at.”

example.en: He arrived at just the right moment.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

example.en: Chess is a game.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.noteEn: Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’

example.en: We have seen that movie.
